ai_patterns_removed: scripture-translation register stripped from Bhishma's speech: 'O tiger of the Kurus', 'O Bharata', 'possessed of little intelligence', 'Madhava is the progenitor as also the destroyer... of the four species' compressed to plain spoken foretelling — dog-and-lion simile and the 'draw that power back into himself' prophecy kept whole

Shishupala's tirade condensed from near-verbatim Ganguli quotation to its four beats (celibacy jab, mocked childhood deeds, the law against striking those who fed or sheltered you, the Amba and brother's-widow charges), cutting ~160 words of 'O Bhishma' refrains and doubled clauses
'affrighting'/'where is thy virtue' archaisms retuned to natural angry speech
rhetorical 'who marvels at that?' and 'what is left of the lesson?' kept as the only two rhetorical turns in the rant
child_friendly_changes: first-reader anchor: Yudhishthira identified as king of the Pandavas performing the Rajasuya, the great sacrifice of an emperor, at Indraprastha
'the regions of Yama' glossed as 'the country of Yama, the king of the dead'
Putana glossed as 'the demoness'; Kamsa charge kept ('whose bread he ate') without explanation of the old feud

Aswa and Vrishava, the kicked cart, Govardhan 'no more than an anthill', the mountain-top meal, the one-sixteenth-of-a-son line — all kept; Amba/Vichitravirya and the brother's-widow charges phrased plainly, no gore
closing keeps the swan-tale beginning and the hushed hall; no moral drawn
risk: Every accusation preserved against the source (MBh 2.40): Bhishma's dogs-versus-sleeping-lion simile ('until he wakes, this king of the Chedis makes all these monarchs look like lions'), Vishnu 'taking back the energy in Shishupala' and the perverse-mind warning, slaying of Putana/Aswa/Vrishava, the cart kicked over, Govardhan held 'like an anthill', the mountain meal, Kamsa 'whose bread he ate', weapons never against women/cows/brahmins or those who fed and sheltered you, Amba carried off though she loved another, Vichitravirya's refusal, sons born to the dead brother's widow, celibacy 'from ignorance or weakness' worth less than a sixteenth of a son, and the swan-sentence 'you shall die at the hands of your own relatives'. Only connective and vocative scaffolding was cut.

ai_patterns_removed: scripture-voice dialogue naturalized: 'O mighty-armed Krishna', 'assurer of all afflicted ones, dispeller of everyone's fear', 'thou art acquainted with morality', 'O tiger of the Yadu race' -> plain plea and plain promise ('I am afraid... grant me a boon' / 'Even when he deserves to be slain, I will pardon a hundred offences of his')
'rendered anxious by affection', 'with great pleasure', 'filled with alarm and anxiety' -> concrete feeling ('torn between love and fear', 'with great joy', 'her joy turned to alarm')
frame re-set so the story opens on the birth, not on an unexplained 'king who now stood raging' dependent on DKS_0391; Bhishma's telling reintroduced only at the close
closing doubled count-line merged to one ('spent one by one... in slights and mockeries and open insults... the count was nearly spent')
child_friendly_changes: opening names the baby Shishupala, the city Chedi, and the future hall at Indraprastha in one breath, so first readers know whose story this is
Krishna introduced with his elder brother Balarama, Dwaraka as 'the city of the Yadavas', and the queen identified as their father's sister — a daughter of the Yadava house
the incorporeal voice, the three eyes/four arms, the braying, the lap-of-a-thousand-kings tour, the arms falling 'like a pair of five-headed snakes', and the third eye fading — all kept plainly
aunt/kinship kept ('What shall I do, aunt?') so the mercy reads as family mercy
risk: Miracle beats preserved verbatim in substance (MBh 2.42): the ass-like cry at birth, parents' resolve to abandon, the bodiless voice's promise that 'the one who is to kill him has already been born', the sign (arms fall like five-headed snakes, third eye vanishes on the slayer's lap), the thousand laps without the sign, the queen herself placing the child on Krishna's lap, and Krishna's exact boon: 'even when he deserves to be slain, I will pardon a hundred offences of his.' The Bhishma-frame and the near-spent count are unchanged in meaning.

ai_patterns_removed: three 'hung in the air' repetitions cut to one (the stone-in-still-water image kept alone); duplicate 'announcement... sacrifice of emperors' beats merged

dangling thread closed: the ending no longer promises 'Uddhava would not be long in answering' without delivering it — the story now ends on Krishna's play-acting question and the decision carried in it
'play within the world of mortals' translationese -> 'what is about to take place among mortals'; 'O God' vocative dropped
Narada's 'hall listened as it had never quite heard anyone speak' meta-aside trimmed
child_friendly_changes: flashback marker added up front ('The story of the great sacrifice had begun in a quieter hall, some time before the kings of the earth gathered at Indraprastha') so readers leaving DKS_0392 are not lost when the scene shifts back to Dwaraka
Dwaraka identified as Krishna's hall and Krishna as the lord of the Yadavas in the opening
Yudhishthira identified as 'the Pandava, your own cousin'; Rajasuya glossed as 'the sacrifice of an emperor'; Uddhava kept as 'his friend and his minister'
Narada's praise of the foot-water kept with the three names glossed by place (Mandakini in heaven, Bhogavati below, Ganga on earth)
risk: Narada's announcement kept whole (BP 10.70.31-46): Krishna's greeting question ('Is there any fear today in the three worlds?'), Narada's praise ('Who can rightly know what you do?... you set free the soul that wanders in ignorance'), the Rajasuya announcement and the purifying power of hearing/chanting/meditating on Krishna, the Mandakini/Bhogavati/Ganga foot-water passage, and Krishna 'receiving it as though it were news' before asking Uddhava — nothing added, no counsel invented.

ai_patterns_removed: translationese dialogue smoothed: 'O tiger among kings', 'Krishna, extolling his virtues', 'it is for thee that the whole earth is under my sway', 'we shall all regard ourselves as crowned with success' -> natural speech keeping every request and promise
'install thyself at that sacrifice' double-option (Krishna installed / Yudhishthira installed) clarified into 'let the sacrifice be yours' vs 'let me be installed at it'
repetitive 'gladdened... gladdened' simile kept once, not twice
child_friendly_changes: Dwaipayana given a role gloss ('the sage Dwaipayana') beside Dhaumya and the priests
brahmanas -> brahmins; 'the fire that carries the offerings' kept as 'the sacred fire'; the wealth and tribute context explained as belonging to Yudhishthira's rule, not greed
Krishna's approval keeps the order that drives the next story: conquer the kings first, gather the requisites, then perform the rite
risk: Krishna's reply preserved in substance (BP 10.72.1-10 + MBh 2.32): Yudhishthira worthy of imperial dignity; conquer all kings and gather requisites, then perform it; 'once it is done, no one will surpass you in splendor, not even the gods'; Krishna always seeking his good and asking for an office in the rite. The 'inexhaustible ocean of gems', the Yadava army left under Vasudeva, the dark-land-gladdened-by-sun simile, and the first order to Sahadeva are unchanged.

ai_patterns_removed: 'the ends of their directions' -> 'the far ends of their roads' (mixed metaphor untangled)
'directions' repeated five times across the piece; varied to quarters/roads/abundance so the motif reads deliberate, not mechanical
closing 'only the great rite itself remained' restored to the strong final position it had lost to a filler sentence
child_friendly_changes: opening glosses who Krishna is and what his permission meant ('the lord of Dwaraka, friend and cousin of the Pandavas... given his blessing to the Rajasuya') so the story stands alone
Srijnayas kept glossed as Sahadeva's allied warriors; each brother's quarter kept concrete (south hot lands, west sea kingdoms and sunset, north mountain passes, east rising sun)
campaigns deliberately left unenumerated exactly as the source leaves them — no invented battles or names
risk: Direction assignments kept exact (BP 10.72.11-13): Sahadeva south with the Srijnayas, Nakula west, Arjuna north, Bhima east; the returns with their tribute (wagons, sea-kingdom wealth, mountain treasure, Bhima's shaking train) and the growing treasury unchanged. No conquest details invented — the source itself records none.

ai_patterns_removed: abstract double opener cut ('The question hung over the great hall the way such a question hangs over any gathering of the powerful...') -> the story now opens on the finished sacrifice and the one honor left
theological shorthand 'lord of the Satvatas' dropped in favor of plain identity ('lord of Dwaraka and of his own clan, the Yadavas') — the epithet added nothing a first reader could use
'seeds of something far worse were already sown' trailer-line replaced by the concrete refusal ('he would not let the worship pass')
closing 'But that is another story' kept once with the image it frames; no second moralizing tag
child_friendly_changes: Shishupala introduced by kingdom ('king of Chedi') where the old text named him bare; Dwaipayana kept as 'the old seer'
arghya explained concretely ('the water and garlands and silk by which a host sets his most honored guest apart'); Rajasuya glossed as the rite that declared Yudhishthira emperor
Yudhishthira's act kept whole: kneeling, washing Krishna's feet, carrying the water to his own head 'as the purest of blessings', yellow silk, garments, jewels; assembly with joined hands

Sahadeva's grounds kept (all deities and every sacrifice have their being in Krishna; one, without a second; soul of all beings, sight undivided) — the theology is the story's point, so it is stated calmly, not cut
risk: Honor scene preserved against BP 10.74.17-28 (Sahadeva's declaration and silence, the assembly's unspoken agreement, Yudhishthira washing the feet and bearing the water on his head, worship with yellow silk and jewels) and MBh 2.36 (Shishupala's pointed roll of the worthier men — Bhishma, Drona, Dwaipayana, Karna — and his 'not even a king' objection). No new argument added to Shishupala's grievance.
